findings.evidence: The people operations office publishes the reimbursement log each quarter. [...] The benefits team publishes the reimbursement log after every open enrollment period.
findings.fix: Name a single office as the publisher of the reimbursement log, state one cadence, and delete the duplicate Overview section's conflicting claim.
findings.location: Program Overview, paragraph 1 and the Overview heading, paragraph 1
findings.violation: Two different terms for the responsible party, the people operations office and the benefits team, are both used for the identical concept of who publishes the reimbursement log, with no signal that they name the same team, and the two passages also disagree on cadence (each quarter versus after every open enrollment period), so a reader cannot tell which office to expect the log from or when.

findings.evidence: If the position counts as full-time, the stipend can apply. If the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, the stipend can apply. If the request arrives before the benefit year ends, the stipend can apply. Only once every condition above is met does the home-office equipment stipend become available to the employee.
findings.fix: State the governing rule first, for example: the stipend applies once the employee is full-time, has completed 90 days of continuous service, and requests before the benefit year ends. Then list the three conditions.
findings.violation: The paragraph opens with three separate conditional sentences that each independently read as sufficient ("can apply"), and only the fourth sentence reveals the governing rule that all three must hold together, forcing the reader to re-read the first three once the conjunctive rule is known.

findings.evidence: How to Apply describes starting a request and a delayed review; Approval Timeline separately states a two-business-day review and a pause-on-incomplete-request rule; Request Steps restates "Completing the request begins with confirming eligibility, and uploading the receipt" as a two-item summary; Program Coordination restates intake-to-payout routing a third time; Review Responsibility adds a previously unmentioned $200 finance-review threshold.
findings.fix: Consolidate How to Apply, Approval Timeline, Request Steps, and Program Coordination into one ordered walkthrough of the request-to-payout sequence, folding Review Responsibility's finance threshold into the same walkthrough at the point it applies.
findings.location: How to Apply, Approval Timeline, Request Steps, Program Coordination, and Review Responsibility
findings.violation: The single task of understanding what happens between submitting a request and getting paid is split across five non-adjacent sections that partially restate and partially extend each other, rather than following the reader's actual step-by-step task sequence in one place, so the reader has to assemble the full process by cross-referencing sections scattered through the rest of the document.

findings.evidence: Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 36 words with 4 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.

findings.evidence: The request is reviewed within two business days.
findings.fix: Rewrite the sentence in active voice, naming the actor that performs the action.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a be-verb plus past-participle passive construction in a context where the actor is recoverable and worth naming directly.

findings.evidence: Also, the deposit happens in order to offset costs the employee already paid at this point in time.
findings.fix: Replace the wordy phrase with its plain equivalent (for example, because for due to the fact that).
findings.violation: The sentence uses a wordy construction from the fixed wordy-phrase list that a shorter equivalent would carry with no loss of meaning.

findings.evidence: However, reimbursement is not available without a completed receipt.
findings.fix: Restate the sentence with at most one negation, or recast it as a positive statement.
findings.violation: 2 negation markers from the fixed negation list co-occur in one clause, so the reader has to work out the statement's logical sign before understanding it.

findings.fix: Replace the heading with text specific enough to be found by scanning.
findings.violation: The heading text matches the fixed list of non-specific heading labels, so a reader scanning headings cannot tell whether the section applies to them.

findings.evidence: The manager approves items pursuant to internal discretion, notwithstanding the standard review checklist.
findings.fix: Replace the jargon term with a plain equivalent, or define it at first use.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a legal or foreign-language jargon term from the fixed list with no plain-language definition in the same or the following sentence.
